I am Diego Filippo Marino. Eigenholm is where I work through the mathematics and engineering of modern machine learning systems in public.

The site sits between a research notebook and a technical journal. I use it to reconstruct papers from their central equations, test implementation details in small experiments, and connect model design to the hardware and numerical constraints that shape it.

## What I write about

My main subject is deep learning, with a particular interest in language models, efficient training and inference, representation learning, and the mathematical structure behind optimization. Scientific computing and numerical methods appear whenever they are the right tools for making an argument concrete.

The site has four sections, divided by what a page is rather than what it is about.

**Writing** is long-form: explanations, and attempts to say something that is not already in the literature. **Projects** turn an idea into an executable model or simulator, the kind of thing that could be lifted into a repository. **Notes** are narrower investigations, derivations, and results that are useful before they grow into a full article. **Replications** attempt to reproduce published results as closely as the available compute and data allow, and each one states up front which numbers it targets, what reproduced, and what did not.

## Method

I prefer primary sources and explicit assumptions. When a result comes from a paper, the page cites it. When a number is illustrative rather than measured on real hardware, it is labelled as such.

Every figure and every quoted number on this site is produced by code that runs when the page is built. Only the snippets that carry an argument appear inline, so what you read is the estimator, the algorithm, or the experiment, and not the axis limits. The rest is folded one click away, the toggle at the top of each page opens all of it at once, and the complete source of any page is linked from that page. Nothing is hidden.

The aim is not to compress a topic into a list of facts. It is to expose the mechanism: what is computed, why the equation has that form, where the memory goes, and under which conditions the method stops helping.
